title: Blood vessels and blood
blurb: Compare arteries, capillaries and veins, name every component of blood, and match ABO and Rh blood types.
question: A patient with type A positive blood needs a red blood cell transfusion. Which donor types are compatible, and why can a type O negative donor give red cells to almost anyone?

teach.h: The pipes and the fluid inside them
teach.body: Blood leaves the heart in arteries, which branch into arterioles, then capillaries, then venules and veins back to the heart. Blood itself is formally a connective tissue: about 55% plasma (the liquid matrix) and about 45% formed elements (cells and cell fragments); that 45% is the hematocrit. In plain English: a network of pipes carries a fluid that is part water and part cargo, with red cells, white cells and platelets riding along.

teach.caption: The aorta is the largest artery and the venae cavae are the largest veins. Veins hold about 60–70% of blood at rest.
Note that each circuit runs artery, then capillary bed, then vein: arteries leave the heart, veins return to it, and exchange happens only in the capillaries.

teach.h: Layers, resistance and the muscle pump
teach.body: Artery and vein walls have three tunics: tunica intima (endothelium), tunica media (smooth muscle and elastic tissue) and tunica externa or adventitia (connective tissue). Capillaries keep only the endothelium, one cell thick, so gases, nutrients and wastes cross easily. Arterioles control resistance and blood pressure by vasoconstriction and vasodilation. In the low-pressure veins, valves and the squeezing of skeletal muscles (the skeletal muscle pump) push blood back toward the heart.

teach.caption: Plasma also carries nutrients, electrolytes, hormones and wastes. Serum is plasma without the clotting factors.
Platelets (thrombocytes) are fragments of megakaryocytes. They form a plug, and fibrinogen becomes a fibrin mesh; vitamin K is needed for several clotting factors.

teach.h: Life of a red blood cell
teach.body: Mature RBCs are biconcave discs with no nucleus, packed with iron-containing hemoglobin. They are made in red bone marrow (hematopoiesis). When oxygen is low, the kidneys release erythropoietin (EPO), which speeds RBC production. Each RBC lives about 120 days; old cells are removed by macrophages in the spleen and liver, and heme is broken down to bilirubin. White blood cells, unlike RBCs, keep their nuclei.

teach.caption: "Never Let Monkeys Eat Bananas." Neutrophils are the first-responder phagocytes; monocytes become macrophages; lymphocytes include B, T and NK cells.

teach.caption: Rh positive means the D antigen is present. An Rh negative person makes anti-D only after exposure to Rh positive blood.

teach.body: Tyler is type A positive. His red cells carry the A antigen and D antigen, and his plasma holds anti-B. He can safely receive red cells from type A or type O donors, Rh positive or negative, because neither carries the B antigen his anti-B would attack. A type O negative unit has no A, B or D antigens on its red cells, which is why O negative is called the universal red cell donor.

teach.text: Type O is the universal DONOR (no antigens); type AB is the universal RECIPIENT (no antibodies). Neutrophils, not lymphocytes, are the most numerous WBC. EPO comes from the KIDNEYS. Veins, not arteries, have valves, and capillaries have one endothelial layer, not three tunics.

items: Arteries: thick walls, high pressure. Capillaries: one endothelial layer, exchange. Veins: valves, low pressure.
Blood: about 55% plasma (92% water; albumin, globulins, fibrinogen) and 45% formed elements.
RBCs: no nucleus, hemoglobin, about 120 days, made in red bone marrow, driven by kidney EPO.
WBC order: neutrophils, lymphocytes, monocytes, eosinophils, basophils.
Platelets plug; fibrinogen becomes fibrin; vitamin K is needed for clotting factors.
O negative = universal RBC donor; AB positive = universal recipient.

summary: You can now compare arteries, capillaries and veins, list the parts of plasma and the formed elements, and rank the white blood cells. You can also trace the life of a red blood cell and decide which ABO and Rh donor types a patient can receive.

A.q: Which vessels are the site of exchange of gases, nutrients and wastes between blood and tissues?
A.why: Capillary walls are a single layer of endothelium, thin enough for gases, nutrients and wastes to cross.

whyNot.1: Arterioles control resistance and blood pressure; their muscular walls are too thick for exchange.
whyNot.2: Venules collect blood after the capillaries; exchange happens in the capillaries themselves.
whyNot.3: Elastic arteries have thick, multilayered walls and carry blood at high pressure, not exchange it.

A.q: Which white blood cell is the most numerous in normal blood?
A.why: Neutrophils make up about 50–70% of white blood cells, the largest share.

whyNot.0: Lymphocytes are second most common, at about 20–40%.
whyNot.1: Monocytes are the largest WBCs, not the most numerous.
whyNot.3: Basophils are the LEAST numerous white blood cells.

A.q: A person with type AB blood has:
options: No antigens, with both anti-A and anti-B
A and B antigens and no ABO antibodies
A and B antigens and both antibodies
No antigens and no ABO antibodies
A.why: Type AB red cells carry both A and B antigens, so the plasma has neither anti-A nor anti-B. That makes AB the universal recipient.

whyNot.0: No antigens with both antibodies describes type O.
whyNot.2: Having anti-A and anti-B would attack the person's own A and B antigens.
whyNot.3: Type AB red cells do carry antigens: both A and B.

B.q: Which feature helps veins return blood from the legs to the heart?
B.why: Venous valves, helped by the skeletal muscle pump, keep blood moving one way toward the heart despite low pressure.

whyNot.0: Thick muscular walls are a feature of arteries; veins have thinner walls.
whyNot.1: A single endothelial layer describes capillaries.
whyNot.2: Pressure in veins is low; ventricular pressure is mostly spent by the time blood reaches them.

B.q: Erythropoietin, which stimulates red blood cell production, is released mainly by the:
B.why: The kidneys release erythropoietin (EPO) when oxygen delivery is low.

whyNot.0: The liver removes old RBCs; it is not the main source of EPO.
whyNot.2: Red bone marrow MAKES the RBCs in response to EPO; it does not release EPO.

B.q: Which plasma protein is the most abundant and helps maintain osmotic pressure?
B.why: Albumin is the most abundant plasma protein and holds water in the blood by osmotic pressure.

whyNot.1: Fibrinogen is the clotting protein that becomes fibrin.
whyNot.2: Globulins include antibodies and transport proteins, but they are not the most abundant.
whyNot.3: Hemoglobin is inside red blood cells, not a plasma protein.

C.q: Andre has type B negative blood and needs red blood cells. Which donor type is compatible?
C.why: Andre's plasma has anti-A, and as an Rh negative person he should not receive the D antigen. O negative red cells carry no A, B or D antigens.

whyNot.0: AB red cells carry the A antigen, which Andre's anti-A would attack.
whyNot.1: B positive carries the D antigen, which can trigger anti-D in an Rh negative person.
whyNot.3: O positive carries the D antigen, so it is not suitable for an Rh negative recipient.

C.q: Which statement about mature red blood cells is CORRECT?
options: They have a nucleus and live about 120 days
They lack a nucleus and live about 120 hours
They are made mainly in the adult liver
They lack a nucleus and live about 120 days
C.why: Mature RBCs have no nucleus and survive about 120 days before macrophages in the spleen and liver remove them.

whyNot.0: Mature RBCs lose their nucleus; white blood cells are the ones with nuclei.
whyNot.1: The lifespan is about 120 DAYS, not hours.
whyNot.2: In adults RBCs are made in red bone marrow; the liver makes them only in the fetus.

C.q: A patient's blood oxygen stays low for several weeks. Which response is expected?
options: More EPO from the liver; more RBCs made
More EPO from the kidneys; more RBCs made
Less EPO from the kidneys; fewer RBCs made
More EPO from the spleen; more RBCs made
C.why: Low oxygen triggers the kidneys to release more erythropoietin, which makes the red bone marrow produce more RBCs.

whyNot.0: EPO comes from the kidneys, not the liver.
whyNot.2: Low oxygen INCREASES EPO release; it does not reduce it.
whyNot.3: The spleen removes old RBCs; it does not release EPO.

reteach.title: A city's roads and traffic
reteach.question: Picture a city: highways out of downtown, tiny driveways at every house, and return roads back in. How do the roads and the traffic match vessels and blood?

blocks.body: Arteries are the high-speed highways leaving downtown (the heart). Capillaries are the narrow driveways where every delivery and pickup happens. Veins are the slower return roads, with one-way gates (valves) so nobody rolls backward. On the roads, red blood cells are delivery trucks carrying oxygen, white blood cells are police and security, platelets are road-repair crews that patch leaks, and plasma is the river of water everything floats along in.

blocks.text: The one-way gates are on the RETURN roads: veins have valves, arteries do not. The deliveries happen only in the driveways: capillaries, not arteries, exchange gases and nutrients.

explain.body: Arteries: thick muscular and elastic walls, high pressure. Arterioles: control resistance and BP. Capillaries: one endothelial layer, exchange, slowest flow. Veins: thinner walls, larger lumen, valves, about 60–70% of blood at rest.

test.q: At rest, where is most of the body's blood volume found?
test.why: Veins hold about 60–70% of the blood volume at rest, acting as a reservoir.

whyNot.0: Arteries hold a smaller share at higher pressure.
whyNot.1: Capillaries are numerous but hold only a small share at any moment.
whyNot.2: The heart chambers hold only a small volume at a time.

explain.body: About 55% of blood. About 92% water, plus albumin (most abundant; osmotic pressure), globulins (antibodies, transport) and fibrinogen (clotting), with nutrients, electrolytes, hormones and wastes. Serum is plasma without clotting factors.

test.q: Serum differs from plasma because serum lacks:
test.why: Serum is the fluid left after blood clots, so the clotting factors, including fibrinogen, have been used up.

whyNot.1: Serum still contains albumin and globulins.
whyNot.2: Serum is still mostly water with dissolved electrolytes.
whyNot.3: Plasma also has no cells, so this is not what distinguishes serum.

explain.body: RBCs: no nucleus, hemoglobin, about 120 days. WBCs: neutrophils (most), lymphocytes, monocytes (largest), eosinophils (parasites, allergy), basophils (least; histamine, heparin). Platelets: fragments of megakaryocytes for clotting.

test.q: Which white blood cell releases histamine and is the least numerous?
test.why: Basophils are the least numerous WBC and release histamine and heparin.

whyNot.0: Eosinophils fight parasites and act in allergy, but they are not the least numerous.
whyNot.1: Neutrophils are the MOST numerous WBC.
whyNot.3: Monocytes are the largest WBC and become macrophages.

explain.body: Type A has A antigens and anti-B; type B has B antigens and anti-A; AB has both antigens and no antibodies (universal recipient); O has no antigens and both antibodies (universal RBC donor). Rh positive means the D antigen is present.

test.q: Type O negative is called the universal red cell donor because its red blood cells have:
options: No A, B or Rh (D) antigens
The D antigen but no A or B
A and B antigens but no D
test.why: With no A, B or D antigens on its red cells, O negative blood gives a recipient's antibodies nothing to attack.

whyNot.0: Carrying A, B and D antigens describes AB positive, the universal RECIPIENT.
whyNot.2: The D antigen with no A or B describes O positive, which can sensitize an Rh negative recipient.
whyNot.3: A and B antigens with no D describes AB negative; a recipient with anti-A or anti-B would attack those cells.
